Linear Algebra: From Vector Intuition to Matrix Factorisations and Data Applications

A text that can be read in order or consulted at any time. The default field is the real numbers; complex numbers are treated separately. Only high-school algebra is needed; the optimisation part uses a little calculus.

Linear algebra studies two kinds of objects: things that can be added and scaled, and maps that preserve those two operations. Matrices are the tool for describing such maps.

On a first reading, take each section in the order intuition → definition → example → compute it yourself. Do not just memorise formulas: when you see a matrix, try to answer at once how it changes space, which equation it corresponds to, and what information it keeps or loses. Suggested three passes:

  1. Build the framework: Sections 1–7 — vectors, bases, matrices, linear systems and rank.
  2. Master the core tools: Sections 8–14 — orthogonality, least squares, determinants, eigenvalues, positive definiteness and the SVD.
  3. Connect to applications: Sections 15–19 — numerical stability, probability and statistics, optimisation, dynamical systems and a worked case.

Contents

  1. Vectors and Basic Operations
  2. Linear Combinations, Span and Independence

Notation

Symbol Meaning
\mathbb R^n space of real column vectors with n entries
x\in\mathbb R^n vectors are column vectors by default
A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n} m rows, n columns; input dimension n, output dimension m
A^T,A^{-1},A^+ transpose, inverse, Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse
I_n,0 identity of order n; zero object whose size is clear from context
\operatorname{Col}(A),\ker(A) column space, null space (also \operatorname{Null}(A))
\operatorname{rank}(A),\operatorname{tr}(A) rank, trace
|x|_2 Euclidean norm
\lambda,\sigma eigenvalue, singular value

Check dimensions first. In Ax=b, A is m\times n, so x must have n entries and b must have m. This catches many errors early.

1. Vectors and Basic Operations

1.1 Three ways to think of a vector

  • Geometric: an arrow in space with direction and length.
  • Computational: an ordered list of numbers.
  • Abstract: an object that can be added and scaled subject to the vector-space axioms.

For example x=(2,1)^T can be a displacement of 2 to the right and 1 up, or the holdings of two assets. The coordinates of a geometric vector depend on the coordinate system; once it is fixed, the vector can be written as a list of numbers.

Vectors need not be arrows: polynomials, functions and matrices also form vector spaces. For instance p(t)=1+2t and q(t)=3-t add to 4+t.

1.2 Addition and scaling

\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\end{pmatrix},\qquad 3\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\3\end{pmatrix}.

Addition superposes two effects; scaling changes magnitude, and a negative scalar also reverses direction. The zero vector is "no net effect" and -x cancels x.

1.3 Length, distance and angle

\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2},\qquad d(x,y)=\|x-y\|_2,\qquad \cos\theta=\frac{x^Ty}{\|x\|_2\|y\|_2}.

For example (1,1)^T and (1,-1)^T have dot product 0, so they are orthogonal. Note that "length" requires a chosen metric; the Euclidean length is just the most common one.

2. Linear Combinations, Span and Independence

2.1 Linear combinations: building new objects from existing directions

For v_1,\ldots,v_k, the expression c_1v_1+\cdots+c_kv_k is a linear combination with arbitrary real coefficients. The set of all linear combinations is the span:

\operatorname{span}(v_1,\ldots,v_k) =\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k c_iv_i:c_i\in\mathbb R\right\}.

One nonzero vector spans a line through the origin; two non-collinear vectors in \mathbb R^3 span a plane through the origin. The zero vector spans only \{0\}.

2.2 Linear independence: is there a direction we can delete?

If c_1v_1+\cdots+c_kv_k=0 has only the solution c_1=\cdots=c_k=0, the vectors are linearly independent; otherwise dependent.

Why does this capture "redundancy"? If some coefficient is nonzero, say c_k\ne0, then

v_k=-\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\frac{c_i}{c_k}v_i,

so v_k can be synthesised from the others and deleting it does not change the span.

Example. v_1=(1,0)^T,v_2=(0,1)^T,v_3=(1,1)^T are dependent since v_3=v_1+v_2. The three vectors span the whole plane but contain only two independent directions.

For two nonzero vectors, "not proportional" suffices for independence; with three or more vectors, pairwise comparison is not enough. In the example, no two vectors are proportional, yet the set is dependent.

2.3 Linear, affine and convex combinations

Type Requirement on the coefficients Geometric meaning
linear none span through the origin
affine \sum_i c_i=1 structure allowing a translation
convex \sum_i c_i=1 and c_i\ge0 segments, triangles, convex hulls

For example (1-t)x+ty traces a segment for t\in[0,1] and the whole line for t\in\mathbb R.

3. Vector Spaces, Subspaces, Bases and Dimension

3.1 What makes a set a vector space

A vector space has addition and scalar multiplication satisfying commutativity and associativity of addition, a zero and negatives, associativity and distributivity of scaling, and 1v=v.

To check that a nonempty subset W of a known vector space is a subspace, verify (1) u,v\in W\Rightarrow u+v\in W and (2) u\in W,c\in\mathbb R\Rightarrow cu\in W; or in one line, au+bv\in W for all u,v\in W and scalars a,b.

Example. W=\{(x,y,z):x+y+z=0\} is a subspace, since linear combinations still satisfy the equation. The set x+y+z=1 misses the zero vector, so it is not a subspace; it is an affine plane.

3.2 A basis: enough and nothing redundant

A set of vectors is a basis of V iff it spans V and is linearly independent. These two conditions guarantee that every v\in V has a unique coordinate representation.

The standard basis e_1=(1,0)^T,e_2=(0,1)^T is a basis of the plane; so is b_1=(1,1)^T,b_2=(1,-1)^T.

Example. Express x=(3,1)^T in the basis B=(b_1,b_2): c_1+c_2=3,\ c_1-c_2=1 gives c_1=2,c_2=1, so [x]_B=(2,1)^T. The vector did not change; its description did.

3.3 Dimension: the number of independent directions

Any two bases of a finite-dimensional space have the same number of vectors, the dimension. For instance \dim\mathbb R^n=n and the plane x+y+z=0 has dimension 2. In an n-dimensional space:

  • more than n vectors are always dependent;
  • fewer than n vectors cannot span the space;
  • exactly n vectors form a basis as soon as either independence or spanning holds.

The space P_d of real polynomials of degree at most d has basis 1,t,\ldots,t^d and dimension d+1. Polynomials of degree exactly d generally do not form a vector space, since the leading terms can cancel under addition.

3.4 Intersection and sum of subspaces

U\cap W contains the directions the two share; U+W=\{u+w\} contains the directions obtainable by combining them.

\dim(U+W)=\dim U+\dim W-\dim(U\cap W).

We subtract the dimension of the intersection because shared directions were counted twice. When U\cap W=\{0\} every decomposition u+w is unique and we write U\oplus W (direct sum). The union of two subspaces is usually not a subspace.

4. Matrices and Linear Maps

4.1 Definition of a linear map

A map T:V\to W is linear if T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v). It preserves addition and scaling and in particular T(0)=0. Rotations, reflections in lines through the origin, scalings and orthogonal projections can all be linear; T(x)=Ax+b is affine when b\ne0.

4.2 What the columns of a matrix tell us

Write A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_n]; then

Ax=x_1a_1+\cdots+x_na_n.

Multiplying a matrix by a vector combines its columns with the input coordinates as weights. Column j is exactly Ae_j, so knowing where the standard basis goes determines the whole map. For example

A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}

sends e_1 to (2,0)^T and e_2 to (1,1)^T, hence (3,2)^T to (8,2)^T.

4.3 Matrix multiplication is composition

If B:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^n and A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m, then AB means "first B, then A":

(AB)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik}B_{kj}.

In general AB\ne BA: rotating then stretching horizontally differs from stretching then rotating. Multiplication is associative and distributive, but the order cannot be swapped freely.

4.4 Transpose and common special matrices

(AB)^T=B^TA^T,\qquad (A+B)^T=A^T+B^T.

A diagonal matrix has possibly nonzero entries only on the diagonal; an upper-triangular matrix is zero below the diagonal; a symmetric matrix has A=A^T; an orthogonal square matrix has Q^TQ=QQ^T=I. Orthogonal matrices preserve length and angle: \|Qx\|_2^2=x^TQ^TQx=\|x\|_2^2. Rotations and reflections are typical.

5. Linear Systems and Gaussian Elimination

5.1 Three readings of one system

Ax=b can be read as: several linear equations; which combination of the columns gives b; which input does the map A send to b. Hence the system is solvable iff b\in\operatorname{Col}(A).

5.2 Why elimination does not change the solutions

On the augmented matrix [A\mid b] use three row operations: swap two rows; multiply a row by a nonzero number; add a multiple of one row to another. All are invertible, so the new system is equivalent.

Worked example.

\begin{cases} x+y+z=6,\\ 2x+3y+z=11,\\ x+2y+3z=14. \end{cases}

Subtract twice row 1 from row 2 and row 1 from row 3 to get y-z=-1,\ y+2z=8. Subtracting the second from the third gives 3z=9, so z=3,y=2,x=1, which satisfies all three original equations.

5.3 Pivots, free variables and the structure of solutions

In row echelon form the first nonzero entry of each nonzero row is a pivot. Pivot columns correspond to basic variables, the others to free variables. Reduced row echelon form also requires pivots equal to 1 with zeros elsewhere in their columns. Three cases:

  • a row [0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c] with c\ne0: no solution;
  • solvable and every variable has a pivot: unique solution;
  • solvable with free variables: infinitely many solutions over the reals.

For example x+y+z=2,\ 2x+2y+2z=4: with y=s,z=t,

x=\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\0\end{pmatrix} +s\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix} +t\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}.

In general, if Ax=b has one particular solution x_p, then all solutions are x=x_p+z,\ z\in\ker(A), because A(x-x_p)=0. The inhomogeneous solution set is in general an affine subspace; the homogeneous one is a subspace.

5.4 LU factorisation: saving the elimination

After suitable row swaps, PA=LU with P a permutation matrix, L unit lower triangular and U upper triangular. To solve, solve Ly=Pb then Ux=y. When many systems share A but have different right-hand sides, the factorisation can be reused.

6. Rank and the Four Fundamental Subspaces

6.1 Rank: the number of independent pieces of information

The rank r equals the dimension of the column space, the dimension of the row space and the number of pivots. For A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n} always r\le\min(m,n). A rank-1 matrix may have many rows and columns but its output varies along a single direction only.

6.2 The four subspaces

Space Definition Lives in Dimension
column space \{Ax:x\in\mathbb R^n\} \mathbb R^m r
null space \{x:Ax=0\} \mathbb R^n n-r
row space \operatorname{Col}(A^T) \mathbb R^n r
left null space \ker(A^T) \mathbb R^m m-r

The rank–nullity theorem is \operatorname{rank}(A)+\dim\ker(A)=n: of the n free input directions, r independently affect the output and n-r are crushed to zero. Moreover

\ker(A)=\operatorname{Col}(A^T)^\perp,\qquad \ker(A^T)=\operatorname{Col}(A)^\perp.

The first is immediate: Ax=0 says x has zero dot product with every row.

6.3 Finding bases in practice

  • Column space: find pivot column numbers by elimination, then take those columns of the original matrix.
  • Row space: the nonzero rows of the echelon form.
  • Null space: solve Ax=0, parametrise the free variables and take the vector multiplying each parameter.
  • Left null space: do the same for A^T.

Row operations preserve the row space and null space but generally change the column space, so the columns of the echelon form must not be used as a basis of the original column space.

Example. For A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\end{pmatrix} the rank is 1; a basis of the column space is (1,2)^T, of the row space (1,2,3)^T, of the null space (-2,1,0)^T,(-3,0,1)^T, and of the left null space (-2,1)^T. The dimensions 1,1,2,1 agree with the table.

7. Invertibility and Change of Basis

7.1 When can a map be reversed

A square matrix A is invertible if there is A^{-1} with A^{-1}A=AA^{-1}=I. Geometrically no direction is lost and every output has a unique input. For an n\times n matrix the following are equivalent:

\begin{aligned} &A\text{ is invertible};\quad \operatorname{rank}(A)=n;\quad \ker(A)=\{0\};\\ &\text{the columns of }A\text{ form a basis of }\mathbb R^n;\quad Ax=b\text{ has a unique solution for every }b;\\ &\det A\ne0;\quad 0\text{ is not an eigenvalue of }A. \end{aligned}

These equivalences are for square matrices. Rectangular matrices may have left or right inverses, but not all of these conclusions carry over.

7.2 Computing and using the inverse

Row-reduce [A\mid I]; if the left half becomes I, the right half is A^{-1}.

\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}^{-1} =\frac1{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix},\quad ad-bc\ne0,
(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1},\qquad (A^T)^{-1}=(A^{-1})^T.

Writing x=A^{-1}b helps in derivations, but in computation one normally calls a linear solver rather than forming the full inverse.

7.3 Change of basis: changing the description

Put the basis vectors in a matrix B=[b_1\ \cdots\ b_n]; then x=B[x]_B and [x]_B=B^{-1}x. If A is the matrix of a transformation in the standard basis, in the basis B it becomes

[T]_B=B^{-1}AB.

This is a similarity transformation. The order of operations: convert new coordinates back to standard ones, apply the map, convert again to the new coordinates. With different input and output bases B and C the matrix is C^{-1}AB, which need not be a similarity.

8. Inner Products, Orthogonality and Projection

8.1 An inner product compares directions

A real inner product is symmetric, bilinear and positive definite. The standard one is \langle x,y\rangle=x^Ty; for a symmetric positive definite M one can also use \langle x,y\rangle_M=x^TMy. Two basic inequalities:

|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\|y\|\ \text{(Cauchy–Schwarz)},\qquad \|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|\ \text{(triangle inequality)}.

The first follows from \|x-ty\|^2\ge0 for all real t; it ensures that the ratio in the angle formula lies in [-1,1].

8.2 Projection: the nearest point in a subspace

Projection of b onto the line through a nonzero vector u:

p=\operatorname{proj}_u b=\frac{u^Tb}{u^Tu}u.

Derivation: require the residual r=b-cu to be orthogonal to u, i.e. u^T(b-cu)=0, and solve for c. Why is it also the nearest point? For any q on the line, p-q lies along the line and r is orthogonal to it, so \|b-q\|^2=\|r\|^2+\|p-q\|^2\ge\|r\|^2.

8.3 Orthonormal bases simplify coordinates

If q_i^Tq_j=0\ (i\ne j) and \|q_i\|=1 the set is orthonormal. Put the vectors as columns of Q\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}; then Q^TQ=I_r. Projection onto their span:

p=QQ^Tb,\qquad P=QQ^T.

A projection matrix satisfies P^T=P,P^2=P; conversely every real symmetric idempotent matrix is the orthogonal projection onto its column space. An idempotent but non-symmetric matrix generally gives an oblique projection. When Q is not square, QQ^T is generally not the identity.

8.4 Gram–Schmidt orthogonalisation

From independent a_1,\ldots,a_r construct an orthonormal basis:

v_k=a_k-\sum_{j<k}(q_j^Ta_k)q_j,\qquad q_k=\frac{v_k}{\|v_k\|}.

At each step subtract the components along earlier directions, then normalise. For example a_1=(1,1)^T,a_2=(1,0)^T give q_1=(1,1)^T/\sqrt2,q_2=(1,-1)^T/\sqrt2. If the input is dependent, some v_k may be 0 and cannot be normalised. In numerical work the more stable modified Gram–Schmidt or Householder methods are used.

9. Least Squares, Regression and QR

9.1 When the equations cannot be satisfied exactly

With noisy data Ax=b usually has no solution. Least squares seeks \widehat x=\arg\min_x\|Ax-b\|_2^2. The goal is for A\widehat x to be the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space, so the residual r=b-A\widehat x satisfies

A^Tr=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad A^TA\widehat x=A^Tb.

These are the normal equations. If A has full column rank, A^TA is positive definite and the solution is unique: \widehat x=(A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb. If the columns are dependent the optimal coefficients may be non-unique, but the fitted values A\widehat x are still unique.

9.2 A complete example: fitting a line

Observations (t,y)=(0,1),(1,2),(2,2), fit y\approx\alpha+\beta t:

A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\quad b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix},\quad A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}3&3\\3&5\end{pmatrix},\quad A^Tb=\begin{pmatrix}5\\6\end{pmatrix}.

The solution is \widehat\alpha=7/6,\widehat\beta=1/2. Fitted values (7/6,5/3,13/6)^T, residual (-1/6,1/3,-1/6)^T. The residuals sum to zero and 0r_1+1r_2+2r_3=0, which is exactly A^Tr=0. The sum of squared residuals is 1/6.

9.3 Least squares by QR

If A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n} has full column rank and m\ge n, the reduced QR factorisation is A=QR with Q^TQ=I_n and R invertible upper triangular. The normal equations become

R\widehat x=Q^Tb,

a single back-substitution. QR avoids forming A^TA and is generally more stable than solving the normal equations directly.

9.4 Weighted least squares and ridge regression

For symmetric positive definite W the weighted objective is (Ax-b)^TW(Ax-b) with normal equations A^TWA\widehat x=A^TWb. Ridge regression penalises large coefficients with \lambda\|x\|_2^2:

\min_x\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2, \qquad (A^TA+\lambda I)\widehat x=A^Tb.

For \lambda>0 the solution is unique even when the columns of A are dependent. In practical regression the intercept is usually not penalised and feature scales matter; these are estimation and modelling choices that linear algebra does not make by itself.

10. Determinants

10.1 The determinant measures signed volume change

For a square A, |\det A| is the volume scaling factor and the sign records whether orientation is reversed. \det A=0 means some direction is flattened. In two dimensions \det=ad-bc. For example \begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix} enlarges areas 6 times; a shear changes shape but not necessarily area.

10.2 Useful properties

\det(AB)=\det A\det B,\quad \det(A^T)=\det A,\quad \det(A^{-1})=(\det A)^{-1}.
  • swapping two rows changes the sign;
  • multiplying a row by c multiplies the determinant by c;
  • adding a multiple of one row to another leaves it unchanged;
  • the determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of the diagonal;
  • for an n\times n matrix, \det(cA)=c^n\det A.

The determinant is linear in a single row or column but not in the whole matrix; in general \det(A+B)\ne\det A+\det B.

10.3 Cofactors and Cramer's rule

Deleting row i and column j gives the submatrix A_{ij} and the cofactor C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}\det A_{ij}; expansion along row i is \det A=\sum_j a_{ij}C_{ij}. If \det A\ne0, replacing column j of A by b gives A_j and x_j=\det(A_j)/\det A. These formulas suit small matrices and theory; large systems use factorisations.

11. Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors and Diagonalisation

11.1 Axes that the map does not turn

If v\ne0 and Av=\lambda v, then v is an eigenvector and \lambda an eigenvalue. A positive eigenvalue scales along the original direction, a negative one also reverses it, and a zero one crushes that direction to zero.

Procedure: solve \det(A-\lambda I)=0, then find \ker(A-\lambda I) for each eigenvalue. Eigenvalues are discussed only for square matrices.

Example. For A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix} the characteristic polynomial is (2-\lambda)^2-1, so the eigenvalues are 3 and 1 with eigenvectors (1,1)^T and (1,-1)^T.

11.2 Diagonalisation: using eigen-directions as axes

If A has n independent eigenvectors, put them as the columns of S; then

A=S\Lambda S^{-1},\qquad \Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n).

Hence A^k=S\Lambda^kS^{-1}: matrix powers become powers of the eigenvalues. Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent, so n distinct eigenvalues guarantee diagonalisability. This is only sufficient: the identity has one distinct eigenvalue and is still diagonalisable.

11.3 Why some matrices cannot be diagonalised

The multiplicity of an eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial is its algebraic multiplicity; the dimension of its eigenspace is its geometric multiplicity. Always

1\le\text{geometric multiplicity}\le\text{algebraic multiplicity}.

When the characteristic polynomial splits completely over the field in use, the matrix is diagonalisable iff the two multiplicities agree for every eigenvalue. For example J=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix} has the single eigenvalue 1 with algebraic multiplicity 2, but its eigenvectors lie only along (1,0)^T, so it is not diagonalisable. Its powers are J^k=\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.

11.4 Trace, determinant and eigenvalues

Counting algebraic multiplicities and allowing complex eigenvalues when needed,

\operatorname{tr}(A)=\sum_i\lambda_i,\qquad \det A=\prod_i\lambda_i.

Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues, trace and determinant; these quantities do not depend on the chosen basis.

12. Symmetric Matrices and the Spectral Theorem

12.1 Why symmetric matrices are so convenient

A real symmetric matrix satisfies the spectral theorem: there are an orthogonal Q and a real diagonal \Lambda with A=Q\Lambda Q^T. All eigenvalues are real and an orthonormal set of eigenvectors can be chosen.

If Au=\lambda u,Av=\mu v, symmetry gives

\lambda u^Tv=(Au)^Tv=u^TAv=\mu u^Tv.

If \lambda\ne\mu then u^Tv=0: directions of different eigenvalues are orthogonal. Within the eigenspace of a repeated eigenvalue one can also orthogonalise.

12.2 The Rayleigh quotient

For nonzero x define R_A(x)=\dfrac{x^TAx}{x^Tx}. In the eigenbasis with x=Qc,

R_A(x)=\frac{\sum_i\lambda_i c_i^2}{\sum_i c_i^2},

a weighted average of eigenvalues: \lambda_{\min}\le R_A(x)\le\lambda_{\max}. On the unit sphere the maximum and minimum are attained at the corresponding eigenvectors. This links PCA and quadratic optimisation directly.

13. Quadratic Forms and Definiteness

13.1 Quadratic forms describe curvature or cost along directions

q(x)=x^TAx. Every real matrix splits into symmetric and antisymmetric parts and x^TAx=x^T\frac{A+A^T}{2}x, so it suffices to study symmetric matrices. In the symmetric case cross terms come in pairs: q(x,y)=ax^2+2bxy+cy^2 corresponds to \begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}.

13.2 Positive definite, semidefinite and indefinite

Assume A=A^T:

Type Condition on vectors Condition on eigenvalues
positive definite x^TAx>0 for every x\ne0 all \lambda_i>0
positive semidefinite x^TAx\ge0 for every x all \lambda_i\ge0
negative definite x^TAx<0 for every x\ne0 all \lambda_i<0
indefinite the form takes both positive and negative values both signs occur

Positive definite means a strictly positive cost in every direction; semidefinite allows zero cost along some nonzero directions. For example A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix} has eigenvalues 3 and 1 and is positive definite; \operatorname{diag}(1,0) is semidefinite but not definite; \operatorname{diag}(1,-1) is indefinite.

13.3 Testing for positive definiteness

A real symmetric matrix is positive definite iff all leading principal minors are positive, i.e. the determinants of the upper-left 1\times1,2\times2,\ldots,n\times n submatrices. For 2\times2: a>0,ac-b^2>0. For semidefiniteness one cannot simply replace ">0" by "\ge0" for the leading minors: semidefinite is equivalent to all principal minors being nonnegative, or to all eigenvalues being nonnegative. For example \operatorname{diag}(0,-1) has all leading minors zero but is clearly not semidefinite.

13.4 Cholesky factorisation and ellipsoids

A positive definite matrix can be written A=LL^T with L lower triangular with positive diagonal, so x^TAx=\|L^Tx\|_2^2. If A=Q\Lambda Q^T is positive definite, the surface x^TAx=1 is an ellipsoid with principal axes along the eigenvectors and semi-axis lengths 1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}. For semidefinite but singular A, not every step of the definite-case Cholesky solution applies; pivoted methods or an eigendecomposition may be needed.

14. The Singular Value Decomposition and the Pseudoinverse

14.1 Rectangular matrices also have natural input and output directions

Every real A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n} has an SVD

A=U\Sigma V^T,

where U,V are orthogonal, \Sigma is an m\times n rectangular diagonal matrix, and the nonnegative singular values are ordered \sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_p\ge0, p=\min(m,n). Read it in order: V^T switches to the natural input directions, \Sigma stretches each or crushes it to zero, U switches to output coordinates. For positive singular values

Av_i=\sigma_i u_i,\quad A^Tu_i=\sigma_i v_i,\quad A^TAv_i=\sigma_i^2v_i.

So singular values are the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of A^TA. This is the way to understand the SVD; numerically one does not usually compute it by forming A^TA.

14.2 The compact SVD and the four subspaces

If the rank is r, keep only the positive singular values:

A=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^T=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i u_iv_i^T.

u_1,\ldots,u_r is an orthonormal basis of the column space and v_1,\ldots,v_r of the row space. The remaining right singular vectors span the null space and the remaining left singular vectors the left null space.

14.3 The pseudoinverse and minimum-norm solutions

Invert the positive singular values and keep the zero ones at zero: A^+=V_r\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r^T. Then x_*=A^+b is always a least-squares solution and has the smallest Euclidean norm among them. All least-squares solutions are

x=A^+b+(I-A^+A)z,\qquad z\in\mathbb R^n,

where AA^+ is the orthogonal projection onto the column space and A^+A onto the row space. If A is invertible, the pseudoinverse is the ordinary inverse.

Example. The equation x_1+x_2=2 has infinitely many solutions. With A=(1\ 1), A^+=(1/2\ 1/2)^T, so the minimum-norm solution is (1,1)^T: the task is shared equally between the two identical directions.

14.4 The best low-rank approximation

Keep the k largest singular values: A_k=\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i u_iv_i^T. Among all matrices of rank at most k it minimises both the Frobenius and spectral error:

\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2,\qquad \|A-A_k\|_2=\sigma_{k+1}.

The latter is used for k<p; keeping all singular values gives zero error. This is the basis of compression, denoising and dimension reduction; if the truncation point has tied singular values the best approximation may be non-unique.

15. Numerical Computation and Condition Numbers

15.1 Exact mathematics versus floating-point computation

A number that is nonzero mathematically may be as small as the rounding error in a computer. "Is it zero?" and "is it full rank?" therefore need tolerances, related to the matrix scale and size, machine precision and noise level in the data. Numerical rank is usually estimated by counting \sigma_i>\tau; one should not apply a fixed absolute threshold to all data.

15.2 Common matrix norms

\|A\|_F=\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2} =\sqrt{\sum_i\sigma_i^2},\qquad \|A\|_2=\max_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Ax\|_2=\sigma_1.

The Frobenius norm treats all entries as one long vector; the spectral norm measures the amplification in the strongest direction.

15.3 The condition number: how much do input errors grow

For an invertible square matrix, \kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}. If only the right-hand side is perturbed, A(x+\delta x)=b+\delta b with b\ne0,

\frac{\|\delta x\|_2}{\|x\|_2} \le\kappa_2(A)\frac{\|\delta b\|_2}{\|b\|_2}.

For example A=\operatorname{diag}(1,10^{-8}) has condition number 10^8: small errors in some directions are visibly amplified.

A small determinant is not a general sign of ill-conditioning. A=10^{-8}I has a tiny determinant but condition number 1, since all directions are scaled equally. Ill-conditioning concerns the relative difference between directions.

15.4 Why not form the normal equations directly

If A has full column rank, \kappa_2(A^TA)=\kappa_2(A)^2, so the normal equations can magnify ill-conditioning. Least squares should usually use QR; for rank-deficient or nearly rank-deficient problems use the SVD or column-pivoted QR.

Distinguish three things: whether the problem itself is sensitive (conditioning), whether the algorithm amplifies extra error (stability), and whether the data support the model (statistical identification and noise). Changing the algorithm cannot repair a lack of information.

16. Probability, Covariance and PCA

16.1 Random vectors and linear maps

Let X\in\mathbb R^p have finite second moments, mean \mu=E[X] and covariance \Sigma=E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T]. It is necessarily symmetric positive semidefinite since w^T\Sigma w=\operatorname{Var}(w^TX)\ge0. If Y=AX+b then

E[Y]=A\mu+b,\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(Y)=A\Sigma A^T.

A constant shift changes the mean but not the covariance. Zero covariance generally does not mean independence; for jointly Gaussian variables, uncorrelated does imply independent.

16.2 Sample covariance and centring

Let the data matrix X\in\mathbb R^{N\times p} have one observation per row and one feature per column. Subtract each column's sample mean to get X_c; the sample covariance is

S=\frac1{N-1}X_c^TX_c,\qquad N>1.

Centring can also be written X_c=HX with H=I_N-\frac1N\mathbf1\mathbf1^T, a symmetric idempotent matrix: the projection onto the subspace orthogonal to the all-ones vector. After centring the rank is at most \min(N-1,p).

16.3 Why PCA looks for eigenvectors

The sample variance after projecting on a unit direction v is v^TSv, so the first principal direction solves \max_{\|v\|_2=1}v^TSv. By the Rayleigh quotient it is the unit eigenvector of the largest eigenvalue. Further components capture the largest remaining variance subject to orthogonality to the earlier ones.

If X_c=U\Sigma_XV^T, the PCA directions are the columns of V, the variances are \sigma_i^2/(N-1) and the scores are X_cV_k=U_k\Sigma_{X,k}. The fraction of variance explained by the first k directions is

\frac{\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i^2}{\sum_i\sigma_i^2},

provided the denominator is nonzero. When features have very different units one must decide whether to standardise, which changes the problem being solved. The direction of maximal variance is not necessarily the most predictive and is not a causal direction.

16.4 Whitening

If the covariance is positive definite with \Sigma=Q\Lambda Q^T, then Z=\Lambda^{-1/2}Q^T(X-\mu) has \operatorname{Cov}(Z)=I. With zero eigenvalues one can whiten only within the nonzero eigen-subspace; very small eigenvalues amplify noise.

17. Matrix Calculus, Optimisation and Portfolios

17.1 A few frequently used derivatives

All gradients are column vectors:

\nabla_x(a^Tx)=a,\qquad \nabla_x(x^TAx)=(A+A^T)x.

For symmetric A the second becomes 2Ax. Hence

\nabla_x\frac12\|Ax-b\|_2^2=A^T(Ax-b),\qquad \nabla_x^2\frac12\|Ax-b\|_2^2=A^TA,

which explains both the normal equations and the convexity of the least-squares objective.

17.2 Quadratic optimisation

For H=H^T consider f(x)=\frac12x^THx-c^Tx. If H is positive definite the objective is strictly convex and the unique minimiser solves Hx=c. If H is only semidefinite there may be many minimisers, or the objective may be unbounded below along a null direction; existence also requires c\in\operatorname{Col}(H). With linear constraints Cx=d the first-order conditions are

\begin{pmatrix}H&C^T\\C&0\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}x\\\nu\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}c\\d\end{pmatrix}.

This is the KKT system for equality constraints. If the constraints are feasible, C has full row rank and H is positive definite on \ker(C), there is a unique constrained minimiser; H need not be positive definite on the whole space.

17.3 The linear algebra of portfolios

This section is a mathematical example, not investment advice. For a random return vector R with mean \mu, covariance \Sigma and weights w: E[w^TR]=w^T\mu,\ \operatorname{Var}(w^TR)=w^T\Sigma w. With \Sigma positive definite, only the constraint \mathbf1^Tw=1 and negative weights allowed, the Lagrange condition of the minimum-variance problem is \Sigma w=\eta\mathbf1, so

w_*= \frac{\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf1}{\mathbf1^T\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf1}.

Example. Two uncorrelated assets with variances 1 and 4, \Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(1,4), give w_*=(4/5,1/5)^T and portfolio variance 4/5.

If weights must be nonnegative, a target return is imposed or other constraints exist, the corresponding constrained problem must be solved; the formula cannot be copied. When the sample covariance is nearly singular, inverting it directly also yields very sensitive weights.

18. Complex Numbers, Dynamical Systems and Further Concepts

18.1 Why complex numbers

The plane rotation matrix R=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix} has no real eigenvalues, but has the complex eigenvalues i,-i. Not every real square matrix has a real eigendirection.

Over the complex numbers use the conjugate transpose A^* instead of the transpose. The standard inner product is x^*y, a Hermitian matrix has A=A^* and a unitary matrix U^*U=I. Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues and are unitarily diagonalisable.

18.2 Discrete-time systems

For x_{t+1}=Ax_t we have x_t=A^tx_0. The spectral radius is \rho(A)=\max_i|\lambda_i|.

  • If \rho(A)<1 every initial state tends to zero, even when A is not diagonalisable.
  • If some |\lambda_i|>1, some initial states grow.
  • If \rho(A)=1 one must also check the Jordan blocks of the eigenvalues on the unit circle; modulus alone does not settle boundedness.

For instance the J above has all eigenvalues 1, yet J^t grows linearly. Even if all eigenvalues have modulus below 1, a non-normal matrix can show a transient amplification early on before decaying.

18.3 Continuous-time systems and the matrix exponential

For \dot x=Ax the solution is x(t)=e^{tA}x(0) with

e^{tA}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.

If A=S\Lambda S^{-1}, then e^{tA}=S\operatorname{diag}(e^{t\lambda_i})S^{-1}. All eigenvalues have negative real part iff this finite-dimensional constant-coefficient system decays exponentially from every initial state.

18.4 Similarity, congruence and other factorisations

  • Similarity S^{-1}AS: the same linear operator in different bases; preserves eigenvalues.
  • Congruence S^TAS: change of coordinates in a quadratic form; for real symmetric matrices it preserves the numbers of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues but not the eigenvalues themselves.
  • Schur decomposition: a complex square matrix is A=QTQ^* with Q unitary and T upper triangular; diagonalisability is not required.
  • Jordan form: describes non-diagonalisable structure via generalised eigenvectors; good for theory, sensitive to small perturbations and usually not the preferred numerical representation.

Further study can turn to bilinear forms, dual spaces, tensor products and operator norms; all build on spaces, bases, inner products and linear maps.

19. A Running Case: From Data to Model

Take the data matrix and observations of Section 9:

A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad b=(1,2,2)^T.

Step 1: identify the spaces. A maps the 2-dimensional parameter space into the 3-dimensional observation space. The first column moves all observations up together; the second controls the linear trend. The columns are independent, so the rank is 2 and the null space is \{0\}.

Step 2: is it exactly solvable? If b were in the column space the three points would be collinear. The two successive slopes are 1 and 0, so no line fits exactly.

Step 3: find the projection. Least squares gives \widehat x=(7/6,1/2)^T; the fitted values lie in the column space and the residual in the left null space.

Step 4: see the orthogonal decomposition. The left null space is one-dimensional, spanned by u=(1,-2,1)^T. The residual is exactly -u/6. Thus b=A\widehat x+r with (A\widehat x)^Tr=0.

Step 5: interpret the residual. u^Tb=1-4+2=-1 measures a discrete second difference. A straight line has zero second difference, so this direction captures precisely the curvature the linear model cannot express.

Step 6: choose an algorithm. By hand one may use the normal equations; in a program prefer QR or a least-squares solver. If a feature equal to twice the second column is added, the parameters become unidentifiable; the pseudoinverse picks the minimum-norm coefficients but cannot create new information.

This small example ties together column space, rank, null space, projection, least squares and model identification.

20. Common Pitfalls and a Route to Solutions

20.1 Easily confused points

Misconception Correct understanding
a vector is a fixed list of numbers distinguish an abstract vector from its coordinates in a basis
pairwise non-proportional implies independent false for three or more vectors
more equations than unknowns means no solution the system may still be consistent; look at rank and right-hand side
fewer equations than unknowns means infinitely many solutions solvability must be guaranteed first
after row reduction take the columns of the echelon form as a column-space basis use the pivot positions to pick columns of the original matrix
AB=AC lets you cancel A needs injectivity or invertibility of A
AB=0 means one factor is zero matrices have zero divisors
a symmetric matrix is positive definite check eigenvalues or an equivalent condition
nonzero eigenvalues imply diagonalisable nonzero only guarantees invertibility
eigenvalues are singular values different in general; they coincide (after sorting) for symmetric positive definite matrices
every projection matrix is QQ^T that is the form of an orthogonal projection
the fitted coefficients give a causal interpretation causal interpretation needs additional identifying assumptions

20.2 Choosing a tool

Problem Starting point Conditions to check
solve Ax=b elimination, LU consistency, uniqueness
find free directions solve Ax=0 number of free variables is n-r
closest fit QR, least squares full column rank, numerical ill-conditioning
minimum-norm solution when rank-deficient SVD, pseudoinverse truncation tolerance vs noise
repeated iteration eigenvalues, Schur moduli, Jordan structure, transient growth
curvature of a quadratic objective symmetric part, eigenvalues definite, semidefinite or indefinite
dimension reduction SVD, PCA centring, units, explained variance
error sensitivity singular values, condition number relative scale and smallest singular value

When learning a new theorem, write down in order: the objects it applies to, the hypotheses, the conclusion, an example, and a counterexample with a hypothesis removed. This is easier to remember than a formula alone.

21. Exercises and Answers

Cover the answers, try to write out the computation, and check against the definitions.

21.1 Exercises

  1. For u=(1,2)^T,v=(3,-1)^T find 2u-v, u^Tv and \|u\|_2.
  2. Are v_1=(1,0,1)^T,v_2=(0,1,1)^T,v_3=(1,1,2)^T independent? Give a basis of their span and an equation for it.
  3. Is W=\{(x,y,z):x-y+2z=0\} a subspace? Find a basis and the dimension.
  4. Solve x+2y+z=3,\ 2x+4y+2z=6, writing the answer as a particular solution plus null-space vectors.
  5. Find the rank and a null-space basis of A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}.
  6. For B=((1,1)^T,(1,-1)^T) find the coordinates of x=(4,2)^T.
  7. Project b=(3,1)^T onto the line spanned by u=(1,1)^T and find the length of the residual.
  8. Fit y=\alpha+\beta t to the data (0,1),(1,1),(2,3) and give the least-squares parameters and residual.
  9. Find the determinant and inverse of \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}.
  10. Find orthonormal eigenvectors of A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix} and decide definiteness.
  11. For which a is the symmetric matrix \begin{pmatrix}1&a\\a&1\end{pmatrix} positive definite, semidefinite, singular?
  12. What is the minimum-norm solution of x_1+2x_2=5?
  13. For \operatorname{diag}(5,2,0) give the rank, the spectral norm and the Frobenius error of the best rank-1 approximation.
  14. For \Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(4,1) give the first principal direction and the fraction of variance explained.
  15. Does x_{t+1}=Ax_t tend to zero from every initial state when A=\operatorname{diag}(0.9,-0.8)? When A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}?
  16. Find the minimiser of f(x)=\frac12x^THx-c^Tx with H=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&4\end{pmatrix},c=(2,8)^T.
  17. Why is A^TA always positive semidefinite? When is it definite? Prove it with quadratic forms.
  18. If P=P^T=P^2, show that Px and (I-P)x are orthogonal and that \operatorname{tr}(P)=\operatorname{rank}(P).

21.2 Answers

1. 2u-v=(-1,5)^T; u^Tv=1; \|u\|_2=\sqrt5.

2. Dependent, since v_3=v_1+v_2. A basis is v_1,v_2; every vector has the form (s,t,s+t)^T, i.e. the equation z=x+y; the dimension is 2.

3. It is the solution set of a homogeneous linear equation, hence a subspace. From x=y-2z a basis is (1,1,0)^T,(-2,0,1)^T; dimension 2.

4. The second equation is twice the first. With y=s,z=t all solutions are (3,0,0)^T+s(-2,1,0)^T+t(-1,0,1)^T.

5. The two rows are independent, so the rank is 2. From y=-z,x=2z a null-space basis is (2,-1,1)^T.

6. Solve c_1+c_2=4,c_1-c_2=2: [x]_B=(3,1)^T.

7. The coefficient is u^Tb/(u^Tu)=4/2=2, so p=(2,2)^T; r=(1,-1)^T has length \sqrt2.

8. A^Tb=(5,7)^T; the normal equations give \widehat\alpha=2/3,\widehat\beta=1. The residual is (1/3,-2/3,1/3)^T, orthogonal to both the constant and the time column.

9. \det A=-2; A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\3/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix}. Multiply back to verify.

10. Eigenvalues 4 and 2 with orthonormal eigenvectors (1,1)^T/\sqrt2 and (1,-1)^T/\sqrt2. All eigenvalues are positive, so A is positive definite.

11. The eigenvalues are 1+a,1-a. Positive definite iff |a|<1, semidefinite iff |a|\le1, singular iff |a|=1; indefinite for |a|>1.

12. The minimum-norm solution is along the normal (1,2)^T; write c(1,2)^T, the constraint gives 5c=5, so the solution is (1,2)^T. Alternatively A^+=A^T/(AA^T).

13. Rank 2, spectral norm 5; the best rank-1 approximation is \operatorname{diag}(5,0,0) with Frobenius error 2.

14. The first direction is (1,0)^T (or its negative); the fraction explained is 4/(4+1)=80\%.

15. The first matrix has spectral radius 0.9, so all states tend to zero. The second has A^t=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}: not all states stay bounded, let alone tend to zero.

16. H is positive definite and Hx=c gives the unique minimiser x=(1,2)^T.

17. x^TA^TAx=\|Ax\|_2^2\ge0. Strict positivity for all x\ne0 holds iff \ker(A)=\{0\}, i.e. A has full column rank.

18. (Px)^T(I-P)x=x^T(P-P^2)x=0. Since P is symmetric it is orthogonally diagonalisable and its eigenvalues satisfy \lambda^2=\lambda, so each is 0 or 1. The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues and the rank is the number of nonzero ones; they coincide.

21.3 Three thought questions

A. What is the difference between unique parameters and unique fitted values? Hint: take A=(1\ 1); the same fitted value arises from different parameters. In general the least-squares fitted value is a unique orthogonal projection; parameter differences lie in the null space.

B. Why can a covariance matrix be singular? Hint: if one feature is an exact linear combination of the others, there is a nonzero w with X_cw=0, hence w^TSw=0. When the number of features p\ge N the centred sample covariance is always singular.

C. Why may an eigenvector change sign, and does a sign flip in PCA matter? Hint: Av=\lambda v also gives A(-v)=\lambda(-v). The PCA direction and scores flip together and the reconstruction is unchanged. For repeated eigenvalues an orthonormal basis inside the eigenspace can additionally be rotated.

22.2 Self-check after finishing

If you can explain these relations without looking at formulas, the core framework is in place:

  1. Why is solving an equation the same as finding a linear combination of columns?
  2. Why does the null space describe the directions in which parameters are unidentifiable?
  3. Why is the least-squares residual orthogonal to the column space?
  4. Why do orthonormal bases simplify coordinates and projections?
  5. Why is eigendecomposition suited to repeated transformations, while the SVD also handles rectangular matrices?
  6. Why is a covariance matrix positive semidefinite, and why does PCA look for the largest-eigenvalue direction?
  7. Why can a theoretically invertible matrix still be hard to solve with reliably?

For any item you are unsure of, return to the example and write your own 2\times2 or 3\times3 instance. You have mastered it only when you can compute, explain and state the conditions of validity.
